verdant

VUR-dnt · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Verdant is green with lush vegetation; covered in rich, healthy plant growth.

The valley was so verdant in early summer that photographers came from hundreds of miles away just to capture its rolling green hills.

Example

After the drought finally broke, the once-dusty fields turned surprisingly verdant within just a few weeks of steady rain.

Verdant describes something rich and green with healthy plant growth -- here, fields transformed from dry and dusty to lush and green.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lush: Lush means rich and abundant — lush growth, lush fabric, even a lush voice — and it is not tied to the color green or to land at all. Verdant is specifically green and almost always describes a landscape: a velvet curtain can be lush, but only countryside is verdant.

leafy: Leafy points at foliage, especially trees — a leafy lane, a leafy suburb shaded by branches overhead. Verdant takes in a whole landscape at once: hills, valleys, and open country covered in rich green growth of every kind, not just places with plenty of trees.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

barren: bare, empty, and without vegetation

arid: extremely dry, with little rainfall or vegetation

Where it sits · how thickly plants take over the land

grassy → verdant → jungle-like

grassy vs. verdant: Something grassy is simply covered in grass, a much plainer image than a fully verdant landscape.

jungle-like vs. verdant: Something jungle-like is thick with dense, tangled, overwhelming plant growth, an even more intense image than merely verdant.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — verd-: green (Latin viridis, via Old French verd)

suffix — -ant: characterized by, full of (Latin)

Put it together: Verdant comes from Old French verd ('green'), itself from Latin viridis. The same verd- root survives in the somewhat rarer English word verdure, meaning lush green vegetation itself.

Use the root in a new word: verdure: The hikers stopped at the overlook to photograph the valley's verdure before the fog rolled in.

Root Check

Word Choice

Verdant almost always describes landscapes -- hills, valleys, forests, fields -- rather than a single plant; you'd call a whole countryside verdant, but you probably wouldn't call one single houseplant verdant.
